subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 24-year-old man is noted to have enlarged, orange-yellow tonsils during a routine examination. He also reports several months of intermittent numbness and tingling of his hands and feet. His HDL cholesterol is 7 mg/dL, LDL cholesterol is 88 mg/dL, and triglycerides are 120 mg/dL. There is no hepatosplenomegaly.
question: Which of the following is the most likely underlying defect?

options.text: Deficiency of cholesteryl ester transfer protein

explanation_correct: Tangier disease is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in ABCA1, the transporter that moves free cholesterol and phospholipid from cells onto nascent apolipoprotein A-I. Without this efflux step HDL cannot mature, so plasma HDL is nearly absent, and cholesterol accumulates in macrophages, producing the enlarged orange tonsils and a peripheral neuropathy.

explanation_incorrect.A: LCAT deficiency (fish-eye disease) also lowers HDL but produces corneal opacities and progressive renal disease rather than orange tonsils with neuropathy.
explanation_incorrect.C: Cholesteryl ester transfer protein deficiency raises HDL cholesterol markedly instead of eliminating it.
explanation_incorrect.D: Apolipoprotein C-II deficiency causes type I hyperchylomicronemia with severe hypertriglyceridemia, not isolated near-absent HDL.
explanation_incorrect.E: NPC1L1 mediates intestinal cholesterol absorption; its inhibition by ezetimibe lowers LDL cholesterol and does not cause absent HDL.

educationalObjective: Tangier disease is caused by ABCA1 mutations and produces near-absent HDL, enlarged orange tonsils, and peripheral neuropathy.
